newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: French audit to set tone for Iberian bonds.
newsitem.headline: French audit to set tone for Iberian bonds.

text.p: The French government's audit of public finances, due on Monday, will set the tone for Spanish and Portuguese bonds next week, analysts said.

If the audit looks unlikely to affect the timing of European Monetary Union (EMU), the Iberian markets will continue their recent firmer trend. However, analysts say the Bundesbank's response to the report will be critical.

If the audit puts the budget deficit at 3.5 percent of GDP or slightly above, but reaffirms a commitment to reach the 3.0 percent level required for EMU by presenting credible measures that do not upset the Bundesbank, Iberia's 10-year spreads with Bunds could near historic lows.
"For a strong Iberia only one thing matters: whether France's deficit will jeopardise implementation of the euro in 1999," said a London investment bank dealer.
Ten-year Spanish and Portuguese bonds have yields of 6.19 percent and 6.25 percent, giving Bund spreads of 63 and 69 basis points respectively.
In mid-June the Bono-Bund spread reached an all-time low of 60 basis points, which compared with the Portuguese historic low of 50 basis points at the end of May.

The French government seems unlikely to accept any new deficit-reducing austerity plan and may turn instead to a mixture of increased corporate taxes and a possible hike in insurance premiums to reduce the deficit.

"These measures may be enough to calm the Bundesbank, which would be all that Portuguese and Spanish bonds would need in order to rise," said Valentin Fernandez, an analyst at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.

"The Bundesbank hasn't talked about the French deficit, which is a good sign. Politicians would rather die than say that there won't be a euro in 1999," said Henrik Lumholdt, a Bank of America analyst in Madrid.
"There may be quite an upbeat mood, though Spanish and Portuguese bonds have already converged a great deal," he added.
Analysts said there would be cause for concern if the Bundesbank did not react favourably to the French deficit announcement and corrective measures.

"If the Bundesbank doesn't like what it sees in France, it could attack and raise the likelihood of a euro postponement. In this case the Iberian countries would suffer most, although less so than Italy," Fernandez said.

"If the Bundesbank threatens to postpone (the euro), then the Spanish Bond-Bund spread could rise above 70 bp, depending on the strength of the threat, though I do not believe this to be likely," he said. -- Lisbon newsroom +(351-1) 3538254
